summary_grc: ὁ Ζεὺς ὅμοιος Ἀμφιτρύωνι γίγνεται· ἡ Ἀλκμήνη δύο παῖδας τίκτει· ὁ Ἡρακλῆς τοὺς δράκοντας ἄγχων διαφθείρει, καὶ ὕστερον τὸν διδάσκαλον τῇ κιθάρᾳ ἀποκτείνει.
summary_en: Apollodorus 2.4.8–9, lightly adapted: every sentence is his, with a few words cut. Zeus takes Amphitryon's shape, the twins Heracles and Iphicles are born, Hera sends two serpents to the cradle, and the young hero kills his music teacher and pleads self-defence. And one sentence asks: was it really Hera's doing?
caption_grc: Ἡρακλῆς διαναστὰς ἄγχων ἑκατέραις ταῖς χερσὶν αὐτοὺς διέφθειρε.

original.note: Apollodorus, Library 2.4.8–9 (to Heracles being sent to the cattle farms), lightly adapted: one story sentence for each sentence of the original, with a few words cut and nothing rewritten. Apollodorus wrote in the 1st or 2nd century AD; the Pherecydes he quotes in sentence 7 was an Athenian writer of the 5th century BC.

sentences.text: πρὸ τοῦ δὲ Ἀμφιτρύωνα παραγενέσθαι εἰς Θήβας Ζεύς, διὰ νυκτὸς ἐλθὼν καὶ τὴν μίαν τριπλασιάσας νύκτα, ὅμοιος Ἀμφιτρύωνι γενόμενος Ἀλκμήνῃ συνευνάσθη καὶ τὰ γενόμενα περὶ Τηλεβοῶν διηγήσατο.

glosses.value: πρὸ τοῦ … Ἀμφιτρύωνα παραγενέσθαι: 'before Amphitryon arrived' (articular infinitive after πρό; Amphitryon was away at war with the Teleboans)
παραγίγνομαι (arrive, be present) | παραγενέσθαι (aorist infinitive)
having made three times as long (τριπλάσιος 'threefold')
lay with her, as if he were her husband (συνευνάζομαι, aorist passive)
the Teleboans, islanders whom Amphitryon was fighting: Zeus even told her the news of the war
διηγέομαι (tell in full) | διηγήσατο (aorist)

sentences.text: Ἀμφιτρύων δὲ παραγενόμενος, ὡς οὐχ ἑώρα φιλοφρονουμένην πρὸς αὐτὸν τὴν γυναῖκα, ἐπυνθάνετο τὴν αἰτίαν·

grammar.md:
**Reading Apollodorus unaided: participles and absolutes.** From this lesson on the story is Apollodorus' own text. Nearly every sentence is built the same way: circumstances first (participles, genitive absolutes), then one main verb.

**1. Count the genitive absolutes.** This passage has four:

| Greek | literally | English |
|---|---|---|
| εἰπούσης δὲ (αὐτῆς) ὅτι … | she having said that … | when she said that … |
| τοῦ δὲ παιδὸς ὄντος ὀκταμηνιαίου | the child being eight months old | when the child was eight months old |
| ἐπιβοωμένης δὲ Ἀλκμήνης | Alcmene calling for help | while Alcmene was calling for Amphitryon |
| τοῦ μὲν Ἰφικλέους φυγόντος, τοῦ δὲ Ἡρακλέους ὑποστάντος | Iphicles having fled, Heracles having stood firm | when Iphicles ran away and Heracles stood his ground |

**2. The articular infinitive with a preposition.** πρὸ τοῦ … παραγενέσθαι 'before arriving': the article τοῦ makes the infinitive a noun, governed by πρό. Its subject is accusative: πρὸ τοῦ Ἀμφιτρύωνα παραγενέσθαι 'before Amphitryon arrived' (Unit 10).

**3. A rationalising variant.** Sentence 7 reports Pherecydes in indirect statement: φησιν Ἀμφιτρύωνα … ἐμβαλεῖν … καὶ … μαθεῖν 'he says that Amphitryon put the snakes in the bed … and learned'. In this version there is no angry goddess: a father makes a cruel test to find out which twin is his. Greek writers from the 5th century on liked to make myths more plausible like this; Palaephatus later wrote a whole book of such explanations.

**4. A list with μέν … δέ.** ἐδιδάχθη … ἁρματηλατεῖν μὲν ὑπὸ Ἀμφιτρύωνος, παλαίειν δὲ ὑπὸ Αὐτολύκου …: one passive verb, five infinitives, five teachers with ὑπό.

culture.title: Heracles goes to school
culture.md:
Athenians loved the idea of the strongest hero as a schoolboy. A red-figure **skyphos by the Pistoxenos Painter** (about 470 BC, now in Schwerin) shows young Heracles walking to his lesson behind an old tattooed Thracian nurse, **Geropso**, who carries his lyre; on the other side his brother Iphicles sits at his lesson with **Linus**. Other cups show the next scene: Heracles smashing a stool or the lyre over his teacher's head.

The story fitted Athenian life. Boys of citizen families learned letters, music (the lyre, and singing the poets) and athletics, often escorted by an enslaved *paidagogos*. Linus' fate made a good joke for teachers and pupils alike.

The lawsuit matters too. Apollodorus says Heracles was acquitted by reading out a law of **Rhadamanthys**: whoever defends himself against someone who started the violence is innocent. Athenian homicide law had a similar idea: killing in self-defence against an attacker was 'lawful killing' and was tried at the court of the Delphinion. The myth borrows the courtroom the audience knew from Unit 11.
